list.listitem: Chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) is a myeloproliferative disorder characterized by the presence of the Philadelphia (Ph) chromosome and the Bcr-Abl mutant gene.

Patients with CML typically present with vague symptoms, such as fatigue or weight loss, or may be asymptomatic. White blood cell count reveals severe leukocytosis with left shift, basophilia and/or thrombocytosis. C
Imatinib, an oral tyrosine kinase inhibitor, is recommended as a standard treatment for chronic phase CML; it delays the progression of the disease. A

Allogeneic stem cell transplantation is still the only curative treatment for CML, but is used as a first-line treatment only in selected patients with high disease risk and low transplantation risk. B

background.definition: Chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) is a clonal hematopoietic stem cell disorder of myeloid lineage. It is defined by the presence of characteristic cytogenetic abnormality—the Ph chromosome—which is a reciprocal balanced translocation between the long arms of chromosome 9 and 22; t(9;22). This results in molecular events associated with Bcr-Abl.

list.listitem: The age-adjusted annual incidence is 1 to 2 cases per 100,000 individuals per year.
Approximately 5000 to 6000 cases of CML are diagnosed annually in the United States.
Before imatinib therapy, the prevalence of CML was approximately 25,000 cases in the United States.

Now that the annual mortality following imatinib therapy has been reduced to 2%, and the prevalence of CML will continue to rise, reaching a plateau in the next 20 years at approximately 250,000 cases. At that point, the annual incidence will equal the annual mortality.
CML accounts for 15% to 20% of cases of leukemia in the United States.
There are no known familial associations in CML. Its risk is not increased in monozygotic twins or in relatives of patients with CML.

Ionizing radiation (exposure to nuclear bombs or accidents; radiation treatment of ankylosing spondylitis and cervical cancer) increases the risk of CML. Its peak incidence is 5 to 10 years after exposure and is dose related.

The risk of CML is not increased in individuals working in the nuclear industry. Radiologists working without adequate protection (before 1940) had an increased risk of developing myeloid leukemia, but no such risk has been found in recent studies.
Benzene exposure increases the risk of acute myelogenous leukemia, but not of CML.
CML is not a frequent secondary leukemia following treatment of other cancers with radiation and/or alkylating agents.
CML is the first neoplastic disease for which a direct chromosomal link was found.

Cytogenetically, CML is characterized in 95% of patients by the presence of the Ph chromosome, a truncated derivative of chromosome 22, a product of the translocation of genetic material between this chromosome and chromosome 9 (t[9;22][q34;q11]). The resulting fusion gene Bcr-Abl codes for an oncoprotein with an unusual tyrosine kinase activity that induces uncontrolled cell proliferation and reduces apoptosis.

The pathogenesis of evolution from chronic phase to advanced phases of CML is not fully understood. The Bcr-Abl gene may acquire new mutations that allow an already genetically unstable phenotype to acquire further changes. A common gene mutation in the evolution from chronic phase to blastic phase involves the p53 gene.
From 30% to 50% of patients with CML are asymptomatic. The most common signs and symptoms include fatigue, abdominal discomfort, splenomegaly, and weight loss.
White blood cell count is usually greater than 50 x 109 cells/L, with a left-shifted differential, basophilia, and thrombocytosis.
CML can be classified into 3 disease phases: chronic, accelerated, and blast.

Confirmation of diagnosis is made by the identification of the Ph chromosome (t(9;22)) by cytogenetic analysis or by the presence of the Bcr-Abl fusion gene by fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) or by reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR).

Differential.Differential_Features: Leukemoid reactions have normal or high leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score
Polycythemia vera, chronic myelomonocytic leukemia, essential thrombocytosis: Ph chromosome negative
Presence of dysplastic features on bone marrow morphologic examination

list.listitem: Diagnosis is made by identification of the Ph chromosome in blood and/or bone marrow, identification of Bcr-Abl transcripts by real-time RT-PCR or FISH, or by HLA typing in patients younger than 65 years.
See for the standard and World Health Organization (WHO) classifications of CML, and for the definitions of treatment response.
Approximately 30% to 50% of patients diagnosed with CML in the United States are asymptomatic. The disease is often detected on routine physical examination or by blood tests.
CML can be classified into three disease phases: chronic phase, accelerated phase, and blast phase. Diagnosis is most commonly made during the chronic phase.

Common signs and symptoms of CML in the chronic phase, when present, result from anemia and splenomegaly. These include fatigue, weight loss, malaise, easy satiety, and left upper quadrant fullness or pain ().

Rare manifestations include bleeding (associated with a low platelet count and/or platelet dysfunction), thrombosis (associated with thrombocytosis and/or marked leukocytosis), gouty arthritis (from elevated uric acid levels), priapism (usually with marked leukocytosis or thrombocytosis), retinal hemorrhages, and upper gastrointestinal ulceration and bleeding (from elevated histamine levels due to basophilia). Leukostatic symptoms (dyspnea, drowsiness, loss of coordination, confusion) due to sludging in the pulmonary or cerebral vessels are uncommon in chronic phase despite white blood cell counts exceeding 100 × 109/L.

Splenomegaly is the most consistent physical sign in CML, and is detected in 50% to 60% of patients. Hepatomegaly is less common (10%-20%). Lymphadenopathy and infiltration of skin or other tissues are uncommon. When present, they favor Ph-negative CML or accelerated or blastic phases of CML. Headaches, bone pain, arthralgias, pain from splenic infarction, and fever are more frequent with CML transformation.
Most patients evolve into the accelerated phase prior to the blastic phase, but 20% transit into the blastic phase without warning.

The accelerated phase may be insidious or may present with worsening anemia, splenomegaly, and organ infiltration. The blastic phase presents as an acute leukemia with worsening constitutional symptoms, bleeding, fever, and infections.

Initial testing when leukemia is suspected should include complete blood count, platelet count, chemistry profile, and bone marrow aspirate and biopsy. The sedimentation rate is usually elevated but this is nonspecific. Bone marrow should be sent for cytogenetics, FISH, RT-PCR,and morphology (percent blasts and basophils).

The diagnosis is confirmed if cytogenetics detect the Ph chromosome (present in 95%) or if FISH and/or RT-PCR detect the presence of the Bcr-Abl fusion gene. Cases of atypical CML (Ph negative and Bcr-Abl negative) are very rare and designated as "atypical CML."
FISH analysis on blood and bone marrow shows a high level of concordance. It has a false positive range of 1% to 10%, depending on the probe used.

RT-PCR on blood and bone marrow also shows high level of concordance and is highly sensitive for the detection of minimal residual disease. It can be either qualitative (diagnosis of CML) or quantitative (monitoring of residual disease and response to treatment).
See for standard WHO classifications of CML.
Confirmation of diagnosis is made by the identification of the Ph chromosome (t(9;22)) and/or Bcr-Abl transcripts (present in 5%) in peripheral blood or bone marrow cells.
See for a suggested approach to treatment.
Imatinib (Gleevec), an oral Bcr-Abl tyrosine kinase inhibitor, is the current first-line therapy for CML in all phases and has dramatically improved outcomes.
With imatinib, overall survival approaches 90% in chronic phase CML patients, but is worse for patients in accelerated and blastic phases. A
Dasatinib and nilotinib are alternative first-line therapies for CML for those patients not tolerating imatinib.A
In cases of imatinib resistance, options include stem cell transplantation (the only curative treatment for CML) and other tyrosine kinase inhibitors, such as dasatinib or nilotinib. B

Historically, CML patients were treated with busulfan (an alkylating agent) and hydroxyurea (an antimetabolite), which had no affect on the disease progression. But interferon alpha improved survival, especially when combined with cytarabine (an antimetabolite cytotoxic agent), and was the standard of care until the introduction of imatinib.

Imatinib (Gleevec) is an oral Bcr-Abl tyrosine kinase inhibitor. It is the current first-line therapy and has dramatically improved outcomes in CML patients. It produced better results than the interferon-cytarabine combination. Imatinib is recommended as first-line therapy by NICE guidelines in the UK as well. A long-term follow-up study (median 11 years) found that the benefit persisted, with a 10 year survival of 83% in treated patients.

Imatinib is approved for CML patients in all phases. The recommended starting dosage in chronic phase CML is 400 mg per day. The most common side effects seen at that dosage include edema and fluid retention, nausea, rash, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, and increased liver enzymes. Severe toxicity is relatively rare at the standard dose.
A small randomized trial (n = 59) assigned patients to imatinib + hydroxyurea or imatinib alone and found no benefit to adding hydroxyurea.

Response to treatment can be defined at the hematologic, cytologic, and/or molecular levels (see ). Treatment with imatinib has consistently led to successful outcomes, with major hematologic response, complete cytogenetic response, and overall survival approaching 90% in chronic phase CML patients. Outcome is worse in patients in accelerated and blastic phases (see ). Higher doses of imatinib (600 mg and 800 mg) can be used in those phases, and are associated with better outcomes.

Imatinib should be started as soon as the diagnosis of CML is made. Allopurinol is recommended until the white blood cell count is less than 10 × 109/L. Tumor lysis syndrome after initiation of treatment is rare. The recommended approach to CML patients depending on response to imatinib is summarized in . If imatinib treatment fails, mutational analysis could identify highly resistant mutants of the kinase domain which would need an alternative treatment strategy. Other mutations may be overcome by increasing the dose of imatinib to 600 mg or 800 mg daily.

In 2013, NICE guidelines, based on a careful systematic review and technology assessment, concluded that nilotinib and dasatinib should be considered as alternative first-line therapies to imatinib for patients with CML not tolerating imatinib.

A recent trial randomised over 400 patients with a new diagnosis of CML to either asciminib or an investigator choice of tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI, a mix of imatinib and second generation TKIs). The outcomes assessed as molecular response at week 48 demonstrated improvement with asciminib compared to imatinib group (67.7% vs. 40.2%).
There is evidence that in chronic phase CML switch from chronic imatinib to nilotanib can increase deep molecular response rate.

After imatinib failure, available therapeutic options include: (1) increasing the dose of imatinib; (2) switching to a second-line agent, such as dasatinib, nilotinib, bosutinib, or MK-0457; (3) allogeneic stem cell transplantation, with conventional or possibly reduced intensity conditioning; (4) classical cytotoxic drugs, eg, cytarabine, hydroxycarbamide (hydroxyurea), busulphan, homoharringtonine, decitabine, arsenicals, or interferon-alfa; (5) experimental agents, such as downstream signal transduction inhibitors (ie, farnesyl transferase inhibitors, mTOR inhibitors, and PI3K inhibitors); (6) autografting with cells collected at diagnosis or after achieving CCyR; and (7) immunotherapeutic strategies.
Patients with largely chronic phase CML and resistance to or side effects from at least two tyrosine kinase inhibitors demonstrated clinical activity in a Phase 2 trial.
Antibiotic prophylaxis is effective in patients undergoing chemotherapy contributing a significant decrease in all cause mortality, with the best evidence favoring quinolones.

Allogeneic bone marrow transplant is the only available curative treatment available for CML patients. However, because of high morbidity and the efficacy of the tyrosine kinase inhibitors, bone marrow transplantation is a second-line therapy. It can still be a first-line therapy in patients with high disease risk and low transplantation risk, or because of patient preferences and economical issues.

Transplantation should also be recommended in cases of imatinib failure due to a T315I mutation, which confers resistance against the FDA-approved tyrosine kinase inhibitors for CML treatment—imatinib, dasatinib, and nilotinib—although some novel agents may show some activity against this specific mutation.
Imatinib therapy should be continued indefinitely.
Treatment discontinuation even among patients with durable complete molecular responses (more than 2 years) has been associated with molecular relapse in approximately half the patients.

DIC may occur in patients with chronic leukemia. Four RCTs with only 126 patients have not identified a clearly effective therapy. Interventions evaluated include human activated protein C, tranxemic acid, dermatan sulfate, and recombinant soluble human thrombomodulin.
If untreated, CML evolves to blastic (myeloid or lymphoid) phase in 3 years to 5 years.
Imatinib has drastically improved the prognosis of patients with CML and has transformed the course of the disease into a long chronic disease with an estimated survival of 25 years.
Follow-up of CML patients and their response to treatment can be done at the hematologic, cytogenetic, and molecular levels with regular bone marrow biopsies and RT-PCR (). C

CML typically evolves in three successive phases: a chronic phase, an accelerated phase, and a blastic phase (). However, some patients may "skip" a phase (ie, go directly from chronic phase to blastic phase).
Without treatment, progression from the chronic phase to the blastic phase generally takes approximately 3 to 5 years.
Approximately two thirds of patients progress to myeloid blastic crisis; the other one third develop lymphoid blastic crisis.
The prognosis for patients with CML has drastically improved in the last decade with the use of imatinib.

Estimated 5-year survival rates for chronic phase CML patients treated with imatinib is 89%. With an annual mortality rate of 1% to 2% in the first 5 years, the estimated median survival of these patients may exceed 25 years.
Survival is also better in patients in accelerated and blastic phases with the introduction of imatinib therapy.
The most relevant prognostic factor of imatinib therapy is the degree of cytogenetic and molecular response to initial imatinib therapy (in the first 3 months to 12 months).
For patients undergoing allogeneic stem cell transplantation, the expected 20-year survival rate is 50% to 60% in younger patients with a matched related donor.
Prognosis is worse in atypical (Ph-negative) CML.
Hematologic response should be checked every 2 weeks until a complete response is achieved, then again every 3 months.
Cytogenetic response should be checked (by bone-marrow aspiration) every 6 months until complete response is achieved, then again at least every 12 months.
If bone-marrow analyses are stopped, changes in differentiation of individual cell lineages, onset of marrow dysplasia, or new cytogenetic aberrations in Ph-negative cells would escape detection.
If a complete cytogenetic remission is achieved, molecular response should be checked every 3 months. The commonly used method is RT-PCR technology.
Mutation analysis should be done if treatment fails, response is suboptimal, or transcript concentrations increase.

If CML is diagnosed in a pregnant woman, she can be managed with leukopheresis if indicated during the first trimester of pregnancy, with hydrea subsequently until delivery, then with more definitive therapy.

Anecdotal reports of successful deliveries after interferon therapy during pregnancy have been reported; however, interferon is antiangiogenic and may have adverse affects on the fetus that are not evident with small numbers.

If a woman becomes pregnant while using imatinib therapy, the drug should be discontinued. Partners of men who are taking imatinib have delivered normal babies. However, the numbers are too small to make definitive conclusions.

cell.label: Chronic myelogenous leukemia, Ph chromosome or BCR-ABL positive. Begin imatinib 400 mg. Hematologic remission at 3 months (see )?
At 6, 12, and 18 months, order bone marrow cytogenetics and assess cytogenetic response (see ).
cell.path: Partial response (6-18 months) or minor response (6 months)
No response, minor response (12-18 months) or relapse (18 months)

cell.label: 6 or 12 months: continue same imatinib dose or increase to maximum 800 mg/day.18 months: change to dasatinib or nilotinib, increase dose of imatinib to maximum 800 mg/day, or consider hematopoietic stem cell transplant.
Assure patient compliance with treatment. Consider mutational analysis. Consider increased imatinib dose vs dasatinib or nilotinib vs hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT).
Monitor peripheral blood with polymerase chain reaction every 3 months for 2 years, then every 6 months for 3 years.
Consider imatinib, dasatinib or nilotinib, interferon, donor lymphocyte infusion, or enrollment in clinical trial.
Repeat bone marrow cytogenetics at 6, 12 and 18 months and reassess (above)
